articles.title: 'Stay humble', Macron tells Le Pen as French vote looms
articles.text:
'Stay humble', Macron tells Le Pen as French vote looms
Advertisement
Politics
'Stay humble', Macron tells Le Pen as French vote looms
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 17 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 16:43 CET
Add a comment
France's President Emmanuel Macron gives a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels. Photo by Ludovic MARIN / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
French President Emmanuel Macron took a swipe at Marine Le Pen Friday, telling the far-right leader, who is the frontrunner in an upcoming presidential election, to "stay humble".
Without naming her directly, Macron criticised recent moves by Le Pen, who laid out plans to cut France's aid to Ukraine and its contribution to the European Union during a visit to Brussels on the eve of an EU leaders summit.
"I'm struck by the lack of humility when some people speak as if they were already in office," Macron told reporters after the EU talks in the Belgian capital.
Advertisement
"Let's show some respect for the men and women of France. They will vote. Stay humble."
France will hold a two-round vote in April and May, after which Macron will exit having serve the maximum two terms as president.
Surveys put Le Pen in the lead to succeed him and in recent days she has been laying out her plans for the country.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
On Wednesday the National Rally party figurehead said Paris would cut financial aid to Ukraine within six months if she is elected -- something Macron retorted would put Europe's security at risk.
"Those who say that we should stop supporting Ukraine and cut off funding are jettisoning the security of Europe and above all, the security of the French people," Macron said.

articles.title: LATEST: Clashes erupt in France on nationwide day of protests
articles.text:
LATEST: Clashes erupt in France on nationwide day of protests
Advertisement
Politics
LATEST: Clashes erupt in France on nationwide day of protests
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 17 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 16:27 CET
1 comment
This photograph shows a burning vehicle during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", at Place de la Republique in Paris on October 17. Photo by Kiran RIDLEY / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
Protesters clashed with police in Paris and other cities in France on Saturday during nationwide rallies over high prices as the country heads towards a presidential election.
French authorities detained dozens across France on on Saturday at the start of nationwide protests against the cost of living, in what is likely to be a key indicator of the social climate heading toward elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Protesters broke into the town hall of France's second-largest city of Marseille before being forced out by police.
Demonstrators also set fire to a tourism office Lyon. The attack occurred in a central square where groups of hooded youths were throwing projectiles and fireworks mortars at the police, who responded with tear gas, dispersal grenades and a water cannon.
Protesters on Saturday smashed their way into the town hall of France's northern city of Lille and vandalised the premises before leaving, an AFP photographer saw.
Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left.
READ ALSO: What are the routes for Saturday's Paris protest?
Advertisement
With just months to go before the two-round elections in April and May to choose Macron's successor, the demonstrations follow weeks of high-school student blockades demanding better learning conditions.
There were clashes at Place de la Republique in Paris where the main demonstration was due to start from at 2pm, whilst violence flared elsewhere in the city where protestors gathered.
Police fired tear gas and used a water cannon against many black-clad protesters, who responded by hurling objects at riot officers. A car was also set ablaze in Place de la Republique.
In Lyon clashes also broke out between police and protesters, with images on French TV showing the city's tourist office vandalised and set on fire.
A protester holds a smoke flare in front of French gendarmes during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", in Bordeaux. Photo by Christophe ARCHAMBAULT / AFP.
Advertisement
The country's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, has called Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in the protests on the first day of half-term holidays.
A protester holds a placard amid tear gas smoke as clashes erupt ahead of a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", at Place de la Republique in Paris on October 17. Photo by Matthieu RONDEL / AFP.
In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.
"We've reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children," he told AFP.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Violence and arrests
In the southern city of Marseille, some protesters attacked a police building, an AFP photographer saw.
Demonstrators clashed with police -- who responded with tear gas -- and briefly blocked a main road with rubbish bins and scooters before officers cleared it.
"We're here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality," said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.
In Paris, where the authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.
Police officers asked passersby for ID outside the Saint-Lazare station, AFP reporters said.
Protesters in balaclavas in the morning threw projectiles and broke windows at the headquarters of the right-leaning television broadcaster CNews.
"It's not just a Yellow Vest movement, it's not just a student movement, it's all the people who are rising up and that's why those in power are afraid," said Benjamin Ball, an activist working on a website for the demonstrations.
A grab from an AFP video shows protesters inside the Marseille's Town Hall. Photo by Viken KANTARCI / AFP.
Advertisement
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to the website set up by organisers.
Around 45 percent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
Macron on Friday evening called "for calm and respect". In Brussels for European Union talks, he added the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property".
The unrest has been seized upon by France's far-left and far-right parties.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.
Le Pen on Saturday accused "rioters" of poisoning cost-of-living protests.
"Looting, pillaging, attacking police -- rioters have once again sullied the October 17 demonstrations over the cost of living" she wrote on X, adding the protesters' demands had been "hijacked by the far left".

articles.title: LATEST: What are the routes for Saturday's Paris protest?
articles.text:
LATEST: What are the routes for Saturday's Paris protest?
Advertisement
Protests
Members only
LATEST: What are the routes for Saturday's Paris protest?
Emma Albright - emma.albright@thelocal.com
Published: 16 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 10:40 CET
Add a comment
A protester holds a placard reading "Money for public services, not for war" as people gather at Place de la Bastille in Paris, on October 14th, 2026. (Photo by MEHDI FEDOUACH / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
A protest against the rising cost of living is expected to take place in Paris on Saturday, October 17th, bringing together students, Gilets Jaunes activists and trade union supporters.
Several demonstrations are planned in Paris on Saturday, October 17th, as part of a national demonstration against the rising cost of living. However, the official protest route remained uncertain until Saturday morning after the Paris police préfecture banned the planned routes over security concerns.
Between 20,000 and 40,000 people are expected to take part in demonstrations in the capital, according to estimates from the authorities - in addition to between 50,000 and 100,000 across the rest of France.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
READ MORE: Blockades and 60 demos: What to expect on Saturday, October 17th in France
What are the planned routes?
A meeting was held on Friday morning between the Paris police prefecture and representatives of Interfacs Île-de-France, the Gilets Jaunes and the CGT trade union. However, no agreement was reached on a definitive protest route.
All groups had called for a joint gathering at Place de la Bastille starting 2pm on Saturday.
“We all agree on where the demonstration should start. The disagreements concern what comes next and where it ends,” Benjamin Ball, creator of the website 17octobregiletjaune.net, told Le Parisien.
In the end an agreement was reached for an official march to start in Place de la Republique and head towards Place de Clichy in the north of the city with a planned departure at 2pm.
The march is set to take Boulevard de Magenta, pass through the Barbès area, and then follow Boulevard de Rochechouart and Boulevard de Clichy towards Place de Clichy. This route will see Gilets Jaunes and labor unions take to the streets.
A second route will see high school and university students from the march between Place de la République and Place de la Nation, via Boulevard Voltaire.
However there were also reports on Saturday morning of unauthorised demonstrations near Gare du Nord with protesters blocked on Rue de Faubourg Saint Denis.
Police have banned gatherings on the Champs-Elysees and in several other parts of the city such as around the ELysée Palace and Nationa Assembly.
Advertisement
Which metro stations could be closed?
The Paris public transport operator RATP announces station closures on the day itself, depending on the situation. Stations along the planned protest routes are the most likely to be affected.
Major disruption and spontaneous gatherings are expected throughout the capital and along major roads. Areas around  Concorde, République, Bastille and Opéra will probably be subject to disruption throughout Saturday.
People planning to attend or travel through central Paris should check the police prefecture's website for the latest information, as routes and meeting points may change - information about closures will also be updated on transport apps such as CityMapper or Google Maps.

articles.title: French word of the Day: Enfariner
articles.text:
French word of the Day: Enfariner
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French word of the Day: Enfariner
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 16 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 10:06 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
The French language is so detailed it even has a word for throwing flour over someone.
Why do I need to know enfariner?
Because it seems to happen a lot lately, especially to politicians.
What does it mean?
Enfariner, roughly pronounced en-fah-ree-nay (listen here), comes from the French la farine - flour - and it means sprinkling flour or white powder over something.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
It can be used when you cook but also when you apply too much makeup powder on your face.
More recently, the term has often been used to describe politicians who have had flour thrown over them.
The latest example was Raphaël Glucksmann, who was covered in flour shortly after being elected the centre-left candidate for France’s 2027 presidential election - he probably won't be the last flour victim during this election campaign.
Embed Youtube Shorts
Raphaël Glucksmann a été enfariné à la sortie du bar de Belleville à Paris, où il célébrait sa victoire au premier tour de la primaire sociale-démocrate. L'identité de l'enfarineur n'est pas encore déterminée. #canal16 #franceinfo https://t.co/RFHFnyIsp4
— franceinfo (@franceinfo) October 11, 2026
But enfariner also has a different, less literal, meaning. It is derived from Se faire rouler dans la farine, a very typical French expression which means to be fooled.
Advertisement
And if it is not flour, politicians can also have a pie thrown in their face. In French, this is known as being entarté.
Use it like this
Je me suis encore fait enfariner ! – I got fooled again!
As-tu bien enfariné le plat avant qu’on verse la pâte dedans ?  - Did you sprinkle enough flour in the dish before we pour the mixture in?
Le politicien s’est fait enfariner le week-end dernier - The politician had flour thrown over him last weekend.
Synonyms
Se faire duper - to be fooled
Saupoudrer de la farine - Sprinkle flour

articles.title: Inside France: Fridges, barricades and a really massive pastry
articles.text:
Inside France: Fridges, barricades and a really massive pastry
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Fridges, barricades and a really massive pastry
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 17 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 11:46 CET
Add a comment
A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on October 12, 2026, following a cyberattack that affected hundreds of supermarkets. Photo by Fred TANNEAU / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From cyberattacks at French supermarkets to the ongoing street protests, via Jordan Bardella memes and a record-breaking French savoury pastry, here's what we have been talking about in France this week.
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.
Cold war
Are fridges the new weapons of war? It's never previously occurred to me to be afraid of a fridge (only angry at it if there inexplicably isn't any wine inside) - but this week France was attacked via the medium of refrigerators.
Hundreds of supermarkets across the country saw their fridge and freezer cabinets suddenly heat up, forcing the stores to throw away millions of euros of food.
The culprit was networked fridges where the temperature can be controlled remotely - hackers had managed to access the systems of two companies, the Danish Danfoss and the American Coupland, that are widely used by French supermarkets and switch them to defrost mode.
READ ALSO: What we know so far about the cyberattack that targeted French supermarkets
Advertisement
At the time of writing, no one has claimed responsibility and the supermarkets have reported receiving no ransom demands.
And France is not the first country where this has happened; Israel saw similar hacks in the spring while US army bases in both Germany and America reported 'unexplained switches to defrost cycles' over the summer.
We don't really know the motive - but if the hackers or their masters intended to show just how vulnerable internet-linked appliances coupled with modern food supply chains make a country, then they certainly succeeded.
As this defence expert put it: "You no longer need tanks to wage war."
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Heating up the streets
If this is all terrifyingly modern, the tradition of French street protest is very old - students, taxi drivers, farmers, union leaders and a few 'yellow vests' are among the groups currently protesting, of which the lycée students are getting the most attention.
Blockades and 60 demos: What to expect on Saturday, October 17th in France
I've noticed among foreigners some surprise that parents have gone along to the lycée student demos with their children (or near them if the teenagers deem it too embarrassing to have their parents there), but I think that is to misunderstand the quasi-sacred role of street protests in France.
The students have the support of a majority of the French population, latest polling shows, and they are also seen as being in the tradition of French protests going right back to the foundation story of the modern republic, the Revolution.
The placard below thanks the 'casseurs' (rioters) at iconic events such as the Storming of the Bastille, the establishment of the Second Republic, the Popular Front and the May 1986 protests.
Regardez cette merveille de pancarte Merci @luciecabiac.bsky.social
[image or embed]
— Mathilde Larrère ( @mathildelarrere.bsky.social) 13 October 2026 at 15:12
Talking France
The Talking France podcast this week attempts to unpick the cyberattacks, as well as what the various presidential election candidates plan for foreigners in France - while we also discuss the risks of moving to France with a French partner. Listen here.
Advertisement
Hero of the week
This French restaurant owner has dedicated almost two years of his life to the logistical and engineering challenges of producing a pâté en croûte that measures more than two metres long. He succeeded, and has now broken the world record for his 2.87m long meaty-pastry delight.
I cannot think of a better way to spend one's fleeting moments upon this earth.
Game of the week
Earlier this week I was searching for a social media post that used the phrase 'ta gueule Jordan' (shut up Jordan, as in Bardella) and to say that I found a lot would be a profound understatement. Obviously some are just people who massively disagree with him, but many others refer to the increasing divides within the Rassemblement National party, with party leaders reportedly keen for the young politico to shut up and go away.
Try it, it's really fun.
Here's Joan of Arc, whose story and image are regularly co-opted by the far right, taking a moment to say 'Shut up Jordan' as she is burned alive.
#DialogueSurToile
[image or embed]
— Bernard-Henri Lemmy ( @bernardhenribery.bsky.social) 3 May 2026 at 10:18
Thanks for reading, and bon weekend
PS: If you like my ramblings, we now have a weekly election newsletter with all the latest from the 2027 campaign trail, plus gossip, scurrilous rumours, memes, etc. Sign up here

articles.title: British travellers warned to avoid scam websites offering Etias visa waiver
articles.text:
British travellers warned to avoid scam websites offering Etias visa waiver
Advertisement
Travel news
British travellers warned to avoid scam websites offering Etias visa waiver
Conor Faulkner - conor.faulkner@thelocal.com
Published: 16 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 17 Oct 2026 10:06 CET
Add a comment
Police officers help passengers to go through a facial recognition verification system at the Terminal 2E of Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport. Photo by Dimitar DILKOFF / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
The rollout of the EU's new Etias visa waiver has been delayed, but fake websites offering the service are catching out British travellers.
Travel experts have warned British nationals not to apply for an Etias visa waiver when travelling to the European Union, as scam websites are already advertising the service despite the rollout being delayed.
ETIAS stands for European Travel Information and Authorisation System and will mean travellers to the EU/Schengen area will need to fill out an online application before they travel.
There is, as yet, no confirmed start date. That is partly due to the fact ETIAS can't be launched until EES is fully in place and the full roll out of the new biometric border checks has repeatedly been delayed or scaled back after travel problems were reported across Europe.
READ ALSO: Europe's airports and airlines demand EES rethink as 'unacceptable' delays continue
Advertisement
In the meantime, travel industry experts are warning British travellers to not fall foul of fake websites, of which there are as many as 150, according to reporting from The Guardian, which are already advertising visa services despite the delay caused by EES backlogs.
Luke Petherbridge, director of public affairs at travel association Abta, told The Guardian: "While Etias was due to come into force this year, it is now back on hold. Abta believes it shouldn’t be brought in until EES is fully operational and working properly."
British travellers unaware of the delay are reportedly falling foul of unofficial websites that employ similar layouts and domain names as official EU web pages.
"If you use one of these sites, not only will you lose money, you are also putting your personal data at risk as well," Petherbridge said. "What I can’t stress is enough that you can’t – and shouldn’t - apply for an Etias now."
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Reiterating the number of sites offering Etias before launch, he added: "This is particularly important when you consider that European authorities believe over 150 websites offering Etias already exist, but there is only one official site people should apply through when live."
According to the most recent update from the official Etias site: "ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point".
"The European Union will inform about the specific date for the start of ETIAS several months prior to its launch."

articles.title: The verdict: Would your life change if the UK rejoined the EU?
articles.text:
The verdict: Would your life change if the UK rejoined the EU?
Advertisement
Reader insights
The verdict: Would your life change if the UK rejoined the EU?
Lana O'Sullivan - lana.osullivan@thelocal.com
Published: 16 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Fri 16 Oct 2026 18:36 CET
1 comment
People wave flags and hold banners during a National 'Rejoin the EU' march in central London on June 20, 2026. (Photo by CARLOS JASSO / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
The UK Prime Minister’s recent hints at rejoining the EU or its single market have sparked debate across Brussels and Westminster. But to what extent would a closer relationship actually change daily life for Brits in Europe? We asked our readers, and here’s what you had to say.
It was the speech that launched a thousand headlines and likely several more eye-rolls across the continent.
Speaking to the BBC at the Labour Party conference, the UK’s newest Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, who only succeeded previous UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July, finally broke a long-standing political taboo in Westminster: Britain’s reentry to the European Union.
Advertisement
It didn’t take long for Europe’s leaders to respond. French President Emmanuel Macron offered a warm "Welcome back" in English, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez promised Spain would open its arms to a "brotherly people".
Official reaction from Brussels remains pragmatic, however. While acknowledging that the shift in tone improves the atmosphere, EU officials insist on clear proposals rather than a return to Brexit-era political infighting.
And, with a recent opinion poll showing over half of UK voters favour rejoining, it’s clear that the debate is far from settled. But, a decade on from the referendum, with post-Brexit life having settled into some kind of norm in most of Europe for a while now, what would a rapprochement—or an eventual return to freedom of movement—actually mean for the millions of Brits living across the EU?
We reached out to British members of The Local’s community to find out.
Get our essential newsletter for Britons living in and moving to Europe
An end to red tape
For many readers, the main draw of returning to the EU is not based on political ideology, but very real, personal day-to-day hurdles.
Under current post-Brexit rules, bringing non-EU spouses to the UK or helping elderly relatives move closer involves income thresholds, health surcharges and strict visa criteria.
"My Swedish partner and I have been together for 35 years", said Samantha, who retired with her partner in Sweden after decades in the UK. "Now that we are retired, we would love to spend much more meaningful time with our Swedish family... without constantly being split up."
Jason, another reader based in Sweden, echoed the sentiment: "My wife and I could move to the UK together without needing to meet any income requirements or paying the NHS tax, or my ageing mother could move over here to be nearer us so we could take care of her."
In France, Louisa highlighted how freedom of movement protects cross-generational care: "My parents could come and live with me at any point if needed, regardless of their dependency on me."
For cross-border families, status discrepancies are also a headache. Eva, who lives in Sweden, pointed out: "Being a family that’s British and Swedish... we have two family members with Settled Status and two with British passports. Rejoining would be far more helpful for EU/British families like ours."
The next generation
While many long-term British nationals in Europe have secured their own residency status through permanent residency or local citizenship, many complain that their children have missed out on full EU rights.
Advertisement
"My kids could have the right to live and work anywhere in Europe, even if they don't get French nationality," said Louisa in France.
In Spain, Andrea shared a similar concern. "My kids, born here with British resident parents, would have freedom of movement again," she said.
For others, regaining EU-wide movement opens up long-delayed plans which impact not just Brits, but their partners and families, too. Simon, a Briton currently based in Australia with his Danish wife, said that a shift in rules "would mean our retirement plans can go ahead—currently, we're not able to easily retire to Denmark."
Banking bother
For many, Brexit introduced daily operational headaches that made even accessing their own money complicated and enjoying the same mundane experiences prohibitively expensive.
Max, who lives in Norway, listed the ongoing "frictions" of post-Brexit life: "Since Brexit, it's become nearly impossible to maintain a UK bank account without jumping through multiple hoops. Car insurance for short trips... has become harder, and restrictions on taking foodstuffs back and forth have become tougher," he said.
Import duties on online shopping and care packages are another common frustration.
Dave in France wished “we could purchase vehicles or buy online without facing import duties again." Ifran in Denmark agreed; "I could get Christmas presents without paying extra delivery tolls... and avoid the process of getting separate passports for the children."
For some British nationals who have become fully integrated in their adopted homeland, such as Debbie in Spain, this is the central metric that would change for them if the UK were to rejoin. She said, "To be fair, living here so long, it wouldn't affect me much other than buying stuff with no import duties."
'Not much would change'
In fact, not every Brit in Europe felt their lives would be transformed if the UK were to rejoin. Particularly for those who have already integrated or secured local citizenship, the practical impact would be minimal.
Jonathan, living in France on a 10-year Carte de Séjour, felt it wouldn't change his daily life "very much at all frankly," though he admitted it would reduce hassle for newcomers. Mark, also in France, added: "Not a lot [would change]
